items.stem: Compare point-source pollution with non-point-source pollution.
items.answer: Point-source pollution comes from a single identifiable outlet (a pipe), so it is easier to monitor and treat; non-point-source pollution comes from diffuse sources (farmland runoff), so it is harder to control.
items.markingKey: Point-source pollution comes from a single identifiable outlet (a pipe), so it is easier to monitor and treat; non-point-source pollution comes from diffuse sources (farmland runoff), so it is harder to control. [1] per valid, explicit comparison up to [3].

items.stem: Distinguish between organic pollution and inorganic pollution.

items.stem: "Eutrophication is caused by toxic chemicals poisoning fish." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Eutrophication is caused by excess nutrients; fish die mainly from oxygen depletion when algae decompose (though some cyanobacteria produce toxins).

items.stem: Distinguish between natural eutrophication and cultural eutrophication.
items.answer: Natural eutrophication is a slow ageing process of lakes over centuries as nutrients accumulate; cultural eutrophication is rapid enrichment caused by human inputs of fertiliser, sewage and detergents.
items.markingKey: Natural eutrophication is a slow ageing process of lakes over centuries as nutrients accumulate; cultural eutrophication is rapid enrichment caused by human inputs of fertiliser, sewage and detergents. items.answer: More of the load was dissolved reactive phosphorus from farm runoff (more bioavailable); warmer water and heavy spring rain favoured cyanobacteria; invasive zebra mussels changed nutrient cycling.

items.stem: A canal draining into the Lagoon of Venice has a nitrate concentration of 12.3 mg/L and a mean discharge of 1.7 m³/s. (1 mg/L = 1 g/m³; there are 86,400 s in a day.) (a) Calculate the daily nitrate load in kg. (b) Calculate the load if catchment measures cut the concentration by 30%. (c) Explain how this nitrate could cause eutrophication downstream and suggest two measures to achieve the reduction.
items.answer: (a) 12.3 g/m³ × 1.7 m³/s × 86,400 s = 1,807 kg per day (b) 1,265 kg per day (c) nitrate fertilises algal growth → algal bloom shades out plants → algae die and are decomposed by bacteria → BOD rises and DO falls → fish die (hypoxic "dead zone"). Measures: buffer strips and wetlands, precision fertiliser application / nitrate vulnerable zones, cover crops, upgrading sewage treatment.
items.markingKey: (a) M1 concentration × discharge × time, A1 1,807. (b) A1. (c) R1 R1 eutrophication sequence, R1 two measures.

items.stem: Suggest three strategies to reduce eutrophication at the stage of nutrient release.
items.answer: Precision fertiliser application and timing; buffer strips and hedges along watercourses; phosphate-free detergents; upgrading sewage works to remove N and P; nitrate vulnerable zones; cover crops.
items.markingKey: Precision fertiliser application and timing; buffer strips and hedges along watercourses; phosphate-free detergents; upgrading sewage works to remove N and P; nitrate vulnerable zones; cover crops.

items.answer: Dead organisms decompose, releasing nutrients and consuming oxygen; low oxygen releases phosphate from sediments (internal loading), fuelling more algal growth and more deaths - the change is amplified.

items.stem: Distinguish between dissolved oxygen and BOD.
items.answer: Dissolved oxygen is the amount of oxygen present in water at a moment; BOD is the amount of oxygen that microorganisms will use to decompose the organic matter present, so it indicates organic pollution load.

items.stem: Families found in a stream survey (BMWP score after each family): Gammaridae (freshwater shrimps): 6; Chironomidae (non-biting midge larvae): 2; Lymnaeidae (pond snails): 3; Glossiphoniidae (leeches): 3; Asellidae (water louse): 3; Baetidae (swimming mayfly nymphs): 4; Oligochaeta (sludge worms): 1. (a) Calculate the BMWP score and the ASPT. (b) Interpret the result and explain why biotic indices complement chemical tests.
items.answer: (a) BMWP = 22; ASPT = 22/7 = 3.1 (b) moderate to poor water quality (ASPT 5 or below); high-scoring taxa (stoneflies, mayflies) need high dissolved oxygen, so their presence or absence integrates water quality over time, whereas a chemical test gives only a snapshot.

items.stem: Describe how a kick-sample could be used to assess the water quality of a stream.
items.answer: Hold a net downstream, disturb the streambed for a fixed time (e.g. 1 minute) over a set area, transfer organisms to a tray, identify to family using a key, calculate a biotic index (BMWP/ASPT), repeat at several sites.

An artificial wetland designed to treat wastewater or runoff by using plants, soil and microbes to remove nutrients and pollutants

items.stem: Explain the difference between cleaning up after pollution and controlling the release of a pollutant.
items.answer: Controlling release stops pollutants reaching the environment (filters, buffer strips, treatment); clean-up removes pollutants or restores ecosystems after damage (dredging, oil-spill dispersants), and is usually more costly and less complete.

items.stem: Briefly explain why clean-up and restoration are the least preferred pollution management strategies.
items.answer: Damage has already occurred, clean-up is expensive and often incomplete, persistent pollutants remain in sediments, and recovery may take decades.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Damage has already occurred, clean-up is expensive and often incomplete, persistent pollutants remain in sediments, and recovery may take decades. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between cultural eutrophication and natural eutrophication.
items.answer: Natural eutrophication is a slow ageing process of lakes over centuries as nutrients accumulate; cultural eutrophication is rapid enrichment caused by human inputs of fertiliser, sewage and detergents.
items.markingKey: Natural eutrophication is a slow ageing process of lakes over centuries as nutrients accumulate; cultural eutrophication is rapid enrichment caused by human inputs of fertiliser, sewage and detergents. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Resource booklet summary (the Great Pacific Garbage Patch): An estimated 80,000 t of plastic is concentrated in the North Pacific Gyre.

Explain what this information reveals about persistent pollution in the oceans.
items.answer: Non-biodegradable plastics are carried by currents and accumulate, fragmenting into microplastics that enter food chains.
items.markingKey: Non-biodegradable plastics are carried by currents and accumulate, fragmenting into microplastics that enter food chains. Award [1] for each valid point linking the extract to persistent pollution in the oceans, up to [4]; at least one point must use detail from the extract.

items.stem: Dissolved-oxygen readings (mg/L) when sampled and after 5 days' dark incubation at 20 °C: above a dairy farm on the River Usk 10.3 → 8.3; below the farm drainage ditch 7.4 → 1.8. Guide: BOD₅ < 3 mg/L clean; 3-5 mg/L moderately polluted; > 5 mg/L polluted. (a) Calculate the BOD₅ at each site and classify the water. (b) Explain why BOD rises downstream of organic pollution. (c) Explain why the samples are incubated in the dark.
items.answer: (a) 2.0 mg/L (clean); 5.6 mg/L (polluted) (b) organic matter (sewage, slurry, pulp) is broken down by aerobic decomposers whose respiration uses dissolved oxygen; more organic matter → more decomposers → greater oxygen demand (and lower DO for fish and invertebrates). (c) to stop photosynthesis by algae adding oxygen, so the fall in DO reflects only respiration.
items.markingKey: (a) A1 2.0, A1 5.6 with classes. (b) R1 decomposition by aerobic microbes, R1 uses DO. (c) R1 prevents photosynthesis.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Baltic Sea Action Plan (HELCOM, 2007) and explain what it reveals about international cooperation in managing water pollution.
items.answer: Baltic states agreed nutrient reduction targets; phosphorus inputs fell by about a quarter, but dead zones persist. Controlling release from sewage works succeeded, but legacy nutrients in sediments and farm runoff slow recovery.
items.markingKey: Context (Baltic states agreed nutrient reduction targets; phosphorus inputs fell by about a quarter, but dead zones persist.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Controlling release from sewage works succeeded, but legacy nutrients in sediments and farm runoff slow recovery. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to international cooperation in managing water pollution.

items.stem: Explain causes and management of eutrophication, referring in detail to Lake Erie, North America and to at least one other example you have studied. [7]
items.answer: Phosphorus inputs caused severe blooms in the 1960s; the 1972 Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement cut phosphorus and the lake recovered, but blooms returned after 2000 and Toledo's water supply was shut for 3 days in 2014. Controlling point sources (detergents, sewage) worked, but rising non-point farm runoff later re-created the problem. A second, contrasting example should be developed in the same way.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Phosphorus inputs caused severe blooms in the 1960s; the 1972 Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement cut phosphorus and the lake recovered, but blooms returned after 2000 and Toledo's water supply was shut for 3 days in 2014. Controlling point sources (detergents, sewage) worked, but rising non-point farm runoff later re-created the problem. items.stem: Suggest two sources of pollution in a river flowing through a large city and one effect of each.
items.answer: Untreated sewage and combined sewer overflows (raised BOD, pathogens); industrial effluent (heavy metals, toxic to fish); urban runoff with oil and microplastics.
items.markingKey: Untreated sewage and combined sewer overflows (raised BOD, pathogens); industrial effluent (heavy metals, toxic to fish); urban runoff with oil and microplastics.

items.stem: Explain water quality indicators and recovery, referring in detail to the Rhine Action Programme and to at least one other example you have studied. [7]
items.answer: After the 1986 Sandoz chemical spill killed fish for hundreds of kilometres, the "Salmon 2000" programme improved water quality and salmon returned. The return of indicator species such as salmon and mayflies shows sustained improvement in water quality. A second, contrasting example should be developed in the same way.

items.stem:
Study the extract from the resource booklet.

Data: a sewage works serving 50,000 people discharges effluent with 8 mg/L phosphate before an upgrade and 1 mg/L after tertiary treatment. Effluent flow is 10,000 m³ per day.

Calculate the reduction in phosphate discharged per day in kg (1 mg/L = 1 g/m³).
items.answer: Before: 8 × 10,000 = 80,000 g = 80 kg; after: 10 kg; reduction 70 kg per day (87.5%).
items.markingKey: Before: 8 × 10,000 = 80,000 g = 80 kg; after: 10 kg; reduction 70 kg per day (87.5%). Award [1] per valid point or correct step, up to [3]; quoted data must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem: Give one strength and one limitation of the claim that reducing nutrient inputs at source is the most effective way to manage eutrophication.
items.answer: Source reduction is essential and most effective long term, but must be combined with restoration where internal loading is high.
items.markingKey: For: tackles the root cause. Against: non-point sources are hard to control. [4]: [1] for a valid argument for and [1] for its development; [1] for a valid argument against and [1] for its development; generic points with no environmental context are capped at [2].

items.stem: With reference to the resource booklet and examples you have studied, evaluate the claim: "Plastic pollution is the most serious threat to marine ecosystems."
items.answer: Plastic pollution is serious and growing, but overfishing, warming and nutrient pollution currently cause greater ecological damage.
items.markingKey: Strengths / supporting points: highly visible, global, persistent; entanglement and ingestion kill marine life. Limitations / counter-points: climate change, overfishing and nutrient pollution cause larger ecosystem-wide damage; acidification affects entire food webs. Conclusion: Plastic pollution is serious and growing, but overfishing, warming and nutrient pollution currently cause greater ecological damage. items.stem: Discuss, from more than one environmental value system, the view that legislation is the most effective way to manage water pollution. [9]
items.answer: Legislation provides the essential framework, but must be combined with funding, incentives for farmers and public action.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: US Clean Water Act (1972) and EU WFD improved many rivers; enforceable standards and fines; polluter pays principle. Arguments challenging it: enforcement varies; many EU rivers still not in good status; non-point sources hard to regulate; needs funding and public cooperation. items.stem: Approximately how many coastal dead zones have been identified worldwide?
options: Over 400
About 5
Over 50,000
About 40
items.answer: Over 400
items.markingKey: A. Diaz and Rosenberg (2008) identified over 400 systems.

items.stem: Which pollutant from mining caused "itai-itai" disease in Japan?
options: Arsenic
Cadmium
Mercury
Lead
items.answer: Cadmium
items.markingKey: B. Cadmium from a zinc mine contaminated rice paddies along the Jinzū River.

items.stem: Define the term "dissolved oxygen (DO)".
items.answer: The concentration of oxygen gas dissolved in water, usually measured in mg/L
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the concentration of oxygen gas dissolved in water, usually measured in mg/L. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Outline why tertiary sewage treatment is important in preventing eutrophication.
items.answer: Primary and secondary treatment remove solids and organic matter but leave dissolved nitrates and phosphates; tertiary treatment removes these nutrients (chemical precipitation, biological nutrient removal) before discharge.
items.markingKey: Primary and secondary treatment remove solids and organic matter but leave dissolved nitrates and phosphates; tertiary treatment removes these nutrients (chemical precipitation, biological nutrient removal) before discharge. [1] per valid point, up to [3].

items.stem: Isabel writes: "Eutrophication is caused by toxic chemicals poisoning fish." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Eutrophication is caused by excess nutrients; fish die mainly from oxygen depletion when algae decompose (though some cyanobacteria produce toxins).
items.markingKey: Eutrophication is caused by excess nutrients; fish die mainly from oxygen depletion when algae decompose (though some cyanobacteria produce toxins). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Plastic pollution comes mainly from ships." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: About 80% of ocean plastic is estimated to come from land-based sources via rivers, coasts and poor waste management.
items.markingKey: About 80% of ocean plastic is estimated to come from land-based sources via rivers, coasts and poor waste management. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Compare direct measurement of pollutants with indirect measurement using indicator species.
items.answer: Direct measurements (nitrate, phosphate, pH, heavy metals) quantify specific pollutants; indirect measurement uses organisms whose tolerance reveals overall water quality over time.
items.markingKey: Direct measurements (nitrate, phosphate, pH, heavy metals) quantify specific pollutants; indirect measurement uses organisms whose tolerance reveals overall water quality over time. [1] per valid, explicit comparison up to [3].

items.stem: "Pollution management is only the responsibility of governments." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Individuals, farmers, industries, NGOs and international bodies all have roles, e.g. consumers choosing phosphate-free detergents.
items.markingKey: Individuals, farmers, industries, NGOs and international bodies all have roles, e.g. consumers choosing phosphate-free detergents. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Ana writes: "Adding more algae-eating fish is the best way to stop eutrophication." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The root cause is nutrient input; reducing inputs at source is essential, although biomanipulation can help restore lakes.
items.markingKey: The root cause is nutrient input; reducing inputs at source is essential, although biomanipulation can help restore lakes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Case study extract - the River Thames, London: Declared "biologically dead" in 1957, it now supports over 125 fish species after sewage-treatment improvements; the Thames Tideway Tunnel (completed 2025) aims to capture sewage overflows.

Using the extract and your own knowledge, explain how this case illustrates monitoring and improving water quality.
items.answer: Reduced organic pollution lowered BOD and raised DO, allowing pollution-sensitive species to return.
items.markingKey: Reduced organic pollution lowered BOD and raised DO, allowing pollution-sensitive species to return. Award [1] for each valid point linking the extract to monitoring and improving water quality, up to [4]; at least one point must use detail from the extract.

items.stem:
Resource booklet summary (the River Thames Tideway Tunnel, London): A 25 km "super sewer" completed in 2025 to capture most of the 39 million tonnes of sewage overflow that entered the Thames in a typical year.

Explain what this information reveals about controlling the release of pollutants.
items.answer: Storing overflow in a tunnel and sending it for treatment stops untreated sewage reaching the river after heavy rain.
items.markingKey: Storing overflow in a tunnel and sending it for treatment stops untreated sewage reaching the river after heavy rain. Award [1] for each valid point linking the extract to controlling the release of pollutants, up to [4]; at least one point must use detail from the extract.

items.answer: Prevention is generally more cost-effective, but clean-up and restoration remain necessary for accidents and legacy pollution.
